content: 1. Denmark was the first country to implement strict regulations on the sale of foods containing trans fats in March 2003, effectively banning partially hydrogenated oils. The limit for trans fats in fats and oils intended for human consumption is set at 2%. This restriction applies to the ingredients rather than the final products, making Denmark the only country where it is possible to consume less than 1 gram of industrially produced trans fats daily, even with a diet including prepared foods. 2. The European Food Safety Authority was tasked with producing a scientific opinion on trans fats. 3. In the United Kingdom, the Food Standards Agency (FSA) called for improved labeling of trans fats in October 2005. An editorial in the British Medical Journal in July 2006 also supported better labeling. By January 2007, major UK retailers, including ASDA, Boots, Co-op, Iceland, Marks & Spencer, Sainsbury's, Tesco, and Waitrose, announced plans to eliminate trans fats from their own-brand products by the end of 2007. Sainsbury's became the first major UK retailer to ban trans fats from all their own-brand foods. 4. In the United States, prior to 2006, consumers could not directly determine the presence or quantity of trans fats in food products, as this information could only be inferred from the ingredient list, particularly from partially hydrogenated ingredients. On July 11, 2003, the FDA issued a regulation requiring manufacturers to list trans fat content on the Nutrition Facts panel of foods and some dietary supplements. Mandatory compliance began on January 1, 2006, with allowances for voluntary compliance earlier. The regulation permits trans fat levels below 0.5 grams per serving to be labeled as 0 grams per serving. However, the FDA did not approve nutrient content claims such as trans fat-free or low trans fat due to the lack of a recommended daily value. The FDA defines trans fats as containing one or more trans linkages not in a conjugated system, distinguishing synthetic trans fats from naturally occurring fatty acids with conjugated trans double bonds, such as conjugated linoleic acid. 5. Critics, including FDA advisor Dr. Carlos Camargo, have expressed concerns that the 0.5-gram per serving threshold is too high to classify a food as free of trans fats, as consuming multiple servings or products could still result in significant trans fat intake. Despite this, the FDA estimated that by 2009, trans fat labeling would prevent 600 to 1,200 cases of coronary heart disease and 250 to 500 deaths annually, primarily due to consumers choosing lower-trans-fat foods and manufacturers reducing trans fat content in their products. 6. Some U.S. cities have taken action to reduce trans fat consumption. In May 2005, Tiburon, California, became the first American city where all restaurants voluntarily cooked with trans fat-free oils. Montgomery County, Maryland, approved a ban on partially hydrogenated oils, becoming the first county in the nation to restrict trans fats. New York City launched a campaign to reduce trans fat consumption, including public education and requests for restaurants to voluntarily eliminate trans fats. When the voluntary program proved unsuccessful, New York City's Board of Health voted on December 5, 2006, to ban artificial trans fats in restaurant food. Restaurants were prohibited from using most frying and spreading fats containing artificial trans fats above 0.5 grams per serving by July 1, 2007, with the same target for all foods by July 1, 2008. Philadelphia also passed a trans fat ban in February 2007, requiring eateries to cease frying food in trans fats by September 1, 2007, and to eliminate trans fats as an ingredient in commercial kitchens a year later. The law does not apply to prepackaged foods sold in the city. Albany County, New York, passed a trans fat ban in May 2007, following New York City's decision, though no implementation plan was established. Chicago and several states, including Massachusetts, Maryland, California, and Vermont, have also considered or implemented trans fat bans. 7. In the food industry, manufacturers have responded to the demand for trans fat reduction. The J.M. Smucker Company reformulated its Crisco shortening in 2004 to contain less than one gram of trans fat per serving while maintaining lower saturated fat content than butter. By January 2007, all Crisco shortening products in the U.S. were reformulated to meet this standard. Unilever eliminated trans fats from all its margarine products in Canada, including its flagship Becel brand, by May 2004. Bunge Limited, through its Bunge Oils division, began producing and marketing a line of non-hydrogenated oils, margarines, and shortenings.
